messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 42
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Project Manager
  trauma_type: Life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 67

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Olfactory (Smell): Related smells, Cold Temperature: Cold, Visual (Needles/Medical): Medical equipment such as needles or drips
  Maladaptive Strategies: Memory Erasure: I try to erase the memory of the event, Thought Monitoring: constantly monitor own thoughts for signs of going crazy, Avoid Medical Cues: Hospitals/ Ambulances/ Physical Examinations
  Memory: Story Feels Unreal: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me, Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory, Partial Clarity: Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank
  Negative Appraisals: Life Destroyed: My life has been destroyed by the trauma, Failed Role: I have failed in my most important role in life, Physical Vulnerability: My body has been permanently damaged by what happened

Vignette:
Mai traces the grain of the wooden armrest in the therapist’s office, a solid, predictable pattern under her thumb. It has been eight months since she was discharged from the hospital, but she feels further from her old life than ever. At forty-two, she had always been the one in control, a successful project manager who mapped out complex timelines and managed risk with an almost preternatural calm. Now, control feels like a distant memory from someone else’s life. The illness had come on with a shocking swiftness—a fever she’d dismissed as the flu, which then exploded into a system-wide infection. Her last clear memory before the ICU was of her husband’s panicked face, and then everything fractured.

Her memory of that time in the hospital is not a coherent story. Instead, it is a collection of searingly vivid fragments surrounded by a grey fog. She can perfectly recall the slick, cold feel of a needle sliding into the back of her hand and the sharp, antiseptic smell of the solution being wiped on her skin. She remembers the exact shade of green on the heart monitor, a jagged line that seemed to be the only thing tethering her to the world. But the hours and days around these moments are completely blank. This fragmentation makes the entire experience feel profoundly unreal, like a terrifying film she was forced to watch. Yet, at other times, the emotional truth of it ambushes her without any image at all. She can be standing in her kitchen and suddenly be gripped by a suffocating, world-ending terror, the pure, distilled feeling of the ICU, even as her eyes see nothing but the familiar tiles and countertops.

In the months since coming home, Mai has dedicated herself to building a fortress against these memories. She actively tries to erase them, pushing down any fragment that surfaces with a force that leaves her exhausted. This began with small things. She threw out all the household cleaners that had that specific, sharp hospital smell. She started taking a longer route to work, a fifteen-minute detour, just to avoid driving past the medical center. She has cancelled her last two physical examinations, the thought of a doctor’s office with its cold rooms and sterile equipment being simply unbearable. Her husband doesn’t understand why she recoils when he turns on a medical drama, or why she insists on keeping the house uncomfortably warm, even in the summer. To Mai, a chill in the air isn’t just a drop in temperature; it’s the ghost of the profound, bone-deep cold she felt while lying helpless under a thin hospital blanket.

This constant vigilance has bled into every corner of her life. At her job, where she once thrived on pressure, she now feels perpetually on edge. The powerful air conditioning in the conference rooms is a constant trigger, making it difficult to concentrate. She finds herself perpetually monitoring her own thoughts, scanning for any sign that she is losing her grip, that the chaos of the illness is seeping into her mind. This internal surveillance makes it impossible to focus on the intricate details of a project plan. She had come to believe her body was permanently damaged by what happened, a fragile system just waiting to fail again. Every minor headache or twinge of fatigue is, in her mind, a harbinger of another catastrophe.

The deepest cut, for Mai, is the sense that she has failed in her most important role. She sees the worry in her husband's eyes and feels a profound sense of shame that she can no longer be the steady, capable partner she once was. She feels like a ghost in her own marriage, present in body but absent in spirit. This conviction solidified a few weeks ago when she missed a critical deadline at work for the first time in her career, a direct result of her inability to focus. Looking at the disappointed faces of her team, she felt a final confirmation of a belief that had been growing for months: her life, the one she had so carefully built, had been destroyed by the trauma. She finally sought help after her husband found her standing frozen in a supermarket aisle, tears streaming down her face, paralyzed by the sight of a display of intravenous drips on a pharmacy advertisement. What brought her to therapy was not just the fear of her triggers, but the terrifying certainty that the capable, confident woman she used to be is gone for good, and a desperate, flickering hope that she might somehow find her way back.
